working_title: Electric vs Push Golf Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Courses
angle: A practical, opinionated decision guide for the regular UK walking golfer who is weighing up whether to upgrade from a push trolley to electric, or buy a push trolley for the first time. Cuts through the marketing noise by focusing on the real factors that matter on British courses specifically: hilly terrain, wet fairways, boot space, charging logistics, and budget.
research_notes:
- The core trade-off: electric trolleys remove the physical effort of pushing but are heavier, bulkier, and need charging between rounds; push trolleys are lighter, more compact, and simpler but require the golfer to do all the work
- UK-relevant terrain note: push trolleys are more appropriate for flatter courses; electric models come into their own on hilly or undulating ground (confirmed by multiple UK sources)
- Body strain consideration: three-wheel push trolleys are easier on the body than old-style two-wheel pull trolleys because the weight is pushed ahead rather than pulled behind — old-style pull trolleys put strain on one side of the body
- Electric trolleys typically weigh 8–12 kg (walk-behind) up to 17 kg (remote control); push trolleys considerably lighter — e.g. PowaKaddy Micra at 7.5 kg
- Walk-behind electric price range roughly £349–£1,349 in the UK market; remote-control models roughly £799–£1,499
- Entry-level electric (£349–£549): reliable lithium battery, simple speed controls, compact fold — suited to first-time electric buyers
- Mid-range electric (£579–£849): more features, better fold, potential GPS integration
- Flagship electric (£1,199+): built-in GPS with yardages to front/middle/back, hazard tracking, downhill braking systems
- Downhill braking (e.g. Motocaddy DHC range) is a meaningful feature for UK parkland and links courses with slopes — worth flagging as a real differentiator
- Remote-control electric models (e.g. Navee Birdie 3, Stewart Golf Vertx, Motocaddy M7 GPS Remote) allow hands-free walking; heavier at 12–17 kg
- Push trolley storage advantage: push trolleys typically include more storage compartments as standard than most electric models
- Key brands in UK market: PowaKaddy and Motocaddy dominate; Stewart Golf, Big Max, Clicgear, MGI also relevant
- Compact fold matters more for electric than push, because the battery makes electric trolleys heavier to lift into the boot
- Lithium batteries: lighter, faster-charging, more reliable than older lead-acid; look for 18-hole or 36-hole capacity depending on how often you play back-to-back
- GPS-equipped trolleys turn the trolley into a performance tool, not just transport — a genuine selling point for golfers who don't use a separate GPS device
- Practical UK logistics: electric trolleys need charging between rounds, which matters for golfers who play multiple days in a row (e.g. on a golf trip) or store their trolley at the club
- For anyone with back or joint issues, electric removes the pushing load entirely across a full round
- Budget verdict from sources: if you play regularly on hilly courses, electric is worth the outlay; if budget is tight or your course is flat, a push trolley is entirely sufficient
